questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not have the opportunity to go travelling during my gap year, so it was really important for me to use this opportunity to travel. I chose Canada because i wanted to explore a country outside of Europe, but still be familiar with the culture and language. I had heard a lot of good things about McGill university and Montréal from older students, and i loved the fact that it was a medium size city.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I absolutely loved everything about it!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I was very lucky to have a friend who went to McGill and Montreal the year before me, who told me a lot. But you get a lot of emails from the university and McGill are hosting several online seminars that you can sign up for, to get information on course registration, health insurance, etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: When I arrived at McGill, all exchange students at the SCIENCE faculty were invited to an information meeting where we got information on course registration, and everyone was encouraged to get a 1 to 1 conversation with the international student secretary - overall i think the information was pretty clear.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my friend who had been the year before me, but many of my friends has found housing through the University and lived on-campus, while many others found it through facebook groups.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Montreal is not that big of a city, so if you live off-campus you won't live more than 30 minutes way in public transport. If you find housing on-campus be aware that many of the other students in the housing will be very social and take up a lot of your time. If you find housing from home via facebook groups, don't hesitate to ask for a FaceTime call to see the apartment. And if you don't find something from home, don't be stressed - everyone will find something eventually.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: All courses will have a 4 letter and 3 digit code (ex. PSYC 311). When you know what courses you want (the full course calendar will be available a few weeks before registration), you have to be ready for when the registration opens. The registrations opens a bit later for exchange students so you need to be fast. You enter the course code and then sign up. If all the spots are full you may be able to join a waitlist, but don't worry - during the first three weeks a lot of people change/drop courses, so if you don't get a spot on your first try, just keep looking for free spots and sign up after the courses have started.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A lot of online videos and seminars were available and did have good instructions on how to sign up for classes.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes i wanted - however i needed to sign up for another time schedule for my FRSL 101 class, because i didn't have time to walk across campus within my 15 minute break :)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Use the visual schedule builder application (website) - you can pan your schedule with the classes you are considering and see how the classes match and add up. Also be aware of the campus and location of the class - you have to run very fast to go from one side of campus to the other in a 10 minute break.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The levels of courses range from 100-600 (or more...) where 100 is the easiest. I had one 100 course, one 300 course, one 400 course and one 500 course. Even though the 100 course was supposed to be the easiest, it was probably one of the classes that i spend more time on - however the academic level was higher on the 500 course. I would recommend only having one 500 course and the some 300 or 400 classes. Then the academic level is fine but you still have the time to go explore.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I had some big classes (more than 300 students) and small classes (15 students). In the big class (PSYC 311) the teaching mostly consisted of weekly lectures and 5 quizzes during the semester with a multiple choice midterm and exam. The smaller classes consisted of more lectures and seminars, where you had to write a term paper and do a presentation about a research article for the whole class. This teaching more resembles the teaching at UCPH. 
I had one french class where the teaching was mostly seminars where we had to prepare weekly homework for each seminar. We also had to do some written and oral assignments and then a 5 minute oral exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PSYC 311 - Human cognition and the brain
PHGY 488 - Stem cell biology 
PHGY 518 - Artifical cells
FRSL 101 - Beginners French 1

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend all my courses. 
PSYC 311 because its more anatomically related. It is a nice break from all the small courses where you go into much detail on the molecular biology. However, there is a lot to remember and the exam is a little tricky with attention to a lot of details. The teacher is really good, and you also look into the clinical use of neuroanatomy and neurophysiology. 
PHGY 488 is a much smaller class with only 15 students. The teaching is very much the same as in Denmark, and the teachers are really good. In the seminars you prepare two research articles pr seminar and present one paper during the semester. You also have to write a term paper on 5 pages about a recent important research article within the field of stem cell biology. The exam consists of essay questions. 
PHGY 518 is tough by a very old man, Professor Chang, who developed the field of artificial cells. It was a topic that i had never heard about before, and to be tough by the man himself was a really nice experience. However, because of his age, the structure of the class is not that great. The PowerPoints are not posted, and the communication between professor and students aren't the greatest. You have to prepare a 10 min presentation and a 10 pages term paper, but there is no exam :) 
FRSL 101 was a really nice break from all the science. Montreal is in the french speaking part of Canada, so it was really nice to learn the basics of the french language. The teachers are really good and its nice with the fellow students because they usually are international students or 1st year students. Be prepared for weekly homework, 4 tests during the semester, oral assignments and a 5 minute interview in the end - but i thought it was really worth it.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not experience any unexpected costs. You pay 7 CAD = 35 DKK for a travel authorization pass which is mandatory.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food was more expensive than expected. Especially vegetables and diary products. However, eating out was cheaper than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are so many clubs and activities to engage in at McGill. There is an outdoors club that arranges so many trips to join for a very small price. Also, there a clubs that will walk or drive you home at night in the weekends for free. There is also a student bar, Gert's, where you can go to many social events or just for a beer after class.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a fitness / gym at the university that arranges several sports to try. You can sign up for yoga classes, squash, badminton, spinning or just a monthly membership at the gym. Also there are so many cultural clubs to join and they do sisal parties where you mostly can just show up. Also the outdoor club is a great opportunity to go on some great trips with other international students. You can also arrange a trip yourself and ask other from the group to join.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: During the first week of uni, there is a 4 day even called FROSH. It is an introduction / orientation event arranged by the different faculties and McGill outdoors club (MOC). Join the MOC FROSH. You can sign up for 4 different trips usually: camping, climbing, hiking and canoeing. The people joining this FROSH are usually older and international students and you get to go on a nice trip and explore the nature around Montreal. When paying for the trip, you are also automatically a member of the MOC. I found some of my best international friends on this trip - we still keep in touch today!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go explore the nature and other cities around Montreal. There are so many beautiful national parks where you could rent a car (MgCill student discount through enterprise) and go for a nice hike. I would also recommend going to Quebec City for a day or two - especially during christmas because they have the cutest christmas markets. I also really enjoyed my trips to Toronto, the Eastern Townships and Vermont. McGill has a club called MustBus that arranges cheap bus rides to some of the big cities during the semester and in the fall-break. Some of the trips are one day and some are with stays. Also just explore Montreal - there are so many things to see and do during all the seasons, so don't feel the need to go on a trip every weekend. Also you have to go watch an ice hockey game with the Montreal team and the McGill team.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Montreal is a very international city with people from all over the world, so it is easy to fit in. You fell the mix of the canadian and the french culture. In some parts of the city, they speak mostly french while other places they speak mostly English. The city have something for everyone - all the seasons, good food, beautiful nature, nice nightlife and bars and very good people.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be shy. Go to some social events arranged by the university, and don't be scared to go alone. A lot of people are coming to Montreal without knowing anyone, so everyone is really friendly and openminded. However, be prepared to fell that it is easier to socialize with other international students-

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: If you dont speak any french, it can be a challenge sometimes. In specific parts of the city they primarily speaks french, so its good to know some basic words for the grocery shopping ;)

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The diverisity of the city - the city has a completely different vibe in all the different parts. I basically felt like i had four cities in one. And all the people are so friendly.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Remember an adapter, passport, yourself and your computer
2) Remember to have fun and not concentrate too much on your studies 
3) Don't be afraid to spend money - you will probably regret it when you come home

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning to navigate in a whole other country and culture without your family or best friends to support you. Even though it sounds terrifying, i learned a lot about my self and what i could handle on my own. I really learned to appreciate time with myself and remembered how good it feels to get to know new people, who doesn't necesarrily come from the same culture as myself.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Adapting to the teaching at a new university. I had gotten so used to the teaching at UCPH, so really had to learn how to prepare for the classes and just do all the classes in another language with students you had never met before. It took me some time to feel confident enough to speak up during my seminars.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
